0.text: The process begins when the customer service representative sends the mortgage offer to the customer. The representative then waits for the customer’s reply. The customer receives the offer and may respond in one of several ways: they can decline the mortgage, send a completed offer with all prerequisites, or send incomplete documents; any of these replies are received at the waiting step and then the response is evaluated. If the customer declines, the representative updates the case details to reflect the decline, archives the case, and cancels it, which ends the process as cancelled. If the customer’s reply is a completed offer with all prerequisites, the representative moves the case to Administration for completion, which triggers Administration to start work; Administration then completes the case and the process ends as completed. If the customer’s reply contains incomplete documents, the representative generates a request for the outstanding documents and sends it to the customer, after which the process returns to waiting for the customer’s reply. If no reply is received within two weeks while waiting, a two-week no-response event occurs, the representative updates the case details accordingly, archives the case, and cancels it, ending the process as cancelled.

1.text: The process starts with the Customer Service Representative sending the mortgage offer to the customer and then waiting for the customer’s response. The customer receives the offer and decides either to decline the mortgage or to send back a completed offer with all prerequisites; in either case, the response is returned to the representative. Based on the response received, the representative either records a declined response, updates the case details, archives the case, and cancels it, which ends the process as archived/cancelled; or proceeds to review the returned documents. After reviewing, if all prerequisites are provided, the representative moves the case to Administration for completion, handing it over and thereby ending the process as handed to administration. If prerequisites are missing, the representative requests the outstanding documents from the customer. The customer receives this request and sends additional documents, after which the representative waits for up to two weeks for these documents. If the documents arrive within the two-week period, the case returns to the document review step. If the documents do not arrive within two weeks, the representative updates the case details, archives the case, and cancels it, ending the process as archived/cancelled.

2.text: The process starts with the Customer Service Representative (CSR) sending the mortgage offer to the customer. The customer receives it and then the CSR waits for the customer’s reply. Depending on what comes back, three outcomes are possible. If the customer declines, the customer sends a decline response to the CSR, who records the decline, updates the case details, and then archives the work and cancels the case, which ends the process. If the customer accepts and sends the completed offer together with all prerequisite documents, the CSR receives the completed documents and moves the case to Administration for completion; the process then ends for the CSR while the handover is communicated to Administration, who completes the administrative processing. If the initial reply is incomplete or missing, the CSR generates a request for outstanding documents and sends it to the customer, then waits two weeks for a response. After this reminder period, either the CSR receives the completed documents and proceeds to move the case to Administration for completion (again informing Administration to complete the administrative processing and ending the CSR’s process), or, if there is still no satisfactory response, the CSR updates the case details and archives the work to cancel the case, which ends the process.

When the CSR receives incomplete documents, they generate a message requesting the outstanding documents and send it to the customer, then wait two weeks for a response. If no response is received within two weeks, the CSR returns to the earlier decision point and re-evaluates the situation (potentially requesting documents again, proceeding to completion if appropriate, or closing the case based on what has been received). The customer receives the offer, after which the CSR waits for one of three possible responses: the customer may decline, send a completed offer with all required documents, or send an incomplete set of documents. If, after requesting outstanding documents, no response is received within two weeks, the CSR updates the case details and archives the work prior to cancellation, ending that path. The communications between participants are as follows: the CSR’s mortgage offer is delivered to the customer; the customer’s decline, completed offer, or incomplete documents are each returned to the CSR; the CSR’s request for outstanding documents is delivered to the customer; the customer’s remaining documents are returned to the CSR; and the CSR’s handover to Administration is delivered for completion.

Based on the received reply, the case follows two main paths. If the reply is a decline, the customer sends a decline back, which is received by the representative; the representative then updates the case details, archives the work, cancels the case, and the process ends. If the reply consists of the customer’s offer documents, the customer sends the documents, which the representative receives and evaluates. After the evaluation, the representative determines whether all prerequisites have been provided. 7.text: In the Customer Service Representative lane, the process begins with sending a mortgage offer to the customer. The customer, in their lane, receives the offer and decides whether to decline or proceed. If the customer declines, they send a decline response back; upon receiving this reply, the representative records the outcome, then archives and cancels the work, and the process ends on their side. If the customer proceeds, they can either send the completed offer with all prerequisite documents or respond later to a request for missing items. When the representative receives a reply that includes all required documents, they move the case to administration for completion and their part ends; this handover is communicated to Administration, where the case is received, the administrative completion is carried out, and that lane then ends. If the representative determines that not all prerequisite documents are present, they request the outstanding documents from the customer. From that point, either the customer responds within two weeks, in which case the representative receives the outstanding documents, moves the case to administration for completion (again triggering the administrative receipt and completion as above), and then ends; or two weeks elapse without a response, after which the representative updates the case and then archives and cancels the work, ending their part. On the customer side, after receiving the offer, sending a decline ends their involvement in that branch; sending the completed offer and prerequisite documents ends that branch as well. Separately, upon receiving the request for outstanding documents, the customer sends the outstanding documents back, which ends that branch on their side. Throughout, communications occur as follows: the offer is sent from the representative to the customer; the customer sends either a decline or a completed-document response back to the representative; if documents are outstanding, the representative requests them from the customer; the customer sends the outstanding documents back; and once the case is moved forward, the representative communicates the handover to Administration, which then completes the case.

Based on the reply, either the case is updated to reflect a decline and the work is archived prior to cancellation, which ends the process, or the reply is treated as an acceptance and the case moves on to an evaluation of whether all prerequisite documents are complete. If everything is provided, the case is moved to Administration for completion and the process ends on the CSR side; at that point, Administration is notified to complete administration for the case. If documents are missing, the representative requests the outstanding documents from the customer and waits two weeks for an answer. If no answer is received within two weeks, the case details are updated accordingly and the work is archived prior to cancellation, ending the process. If the answer arrives within the two-week period, the outstanding documents are received and the case returns to the completeness evaluation, repeating this cycle until all prerequisites are satisfied and the case is handed over to Administration. 9.text: The process begins with the Customer Service Representative sending the mortgage offer to the customer. Upon receiving the offer, the customer reviews it and decides either to decline, to accept by sending a completed offer with all prerequisite documents, or to send documents that are still missing some prerequisites. If the customer declines, the decline is received by the representative, who then updates the case details and archives and cancels the case, ending the process as canceled. If the customer sends documents, the representative receives them and checks whether all prerequisite documents have been provided: when everything is complete, the representative moves the case to Administration for completion and concludes the representative’s work as sent to administration; this handover triggers Administration to receive the case, complete the administration procedures, and finish. If the documents are incomplete, the representative requests the outstanding items from the customer and then waits up to two weeks for a response. If no response is received within that period, the representative updates the case details and archives and cancels the case, ending as canceled. If a response arrives in time, the customer’s outstanding documents are received by the representative, who again treats them as incoming documents and rechecks whether all prerequisites are now satisfied, proceeding either to send the case to Administration when complete or to repeat the request-and-wait cycle if items are still missing. All communications occur via messages: the offer is sent to the customer; a decline, a completed document package, or an incomplete document set is sent back to the representative; requests for outstanding documents are sent to the customer, who then sends the outstanding documents back; and when the case is ready for completion, the representative sends it to Administration, which confirms receipt and completes the administrative work.

0.text: The process starts when Sales receives an order and evaluates it to decide whether to accept or reject it. If the order is rejected, the process ends immediately. If it is accepted, Sales informs the Storehouse and Engineering at the same time. On the Storehouse side, after being informed of the order, the required quantity is checked for an item; if the item is available in-house, it is reserved, otherwise it is back-ordered. After handling the item, a decision is made whether there are more items on the parts list: if there are, the required quantity is checked for the next item and the same availability decision and reserve/back-order handling repeats until all items have been processed; when there are no more items, the Storehouse branch is considered finished. In parallel, Engineering, after being informed of the order, prepares the assembly. Once both the Storehouse has finished processing all items and Engineering has finished preparation, the bicycle is assembled, then shipped to the customer, and the process ends.

0.text: The process starts in room service when the manager begins handling a new request, while a guest calls room service and communicates the order to the manager, who takes it down. Based on what was ordered, the manager submits an order ticket to the kitchen for food, gives the order to the sommelier if alcoholic beverages are included, and assigns the order to a waiter. The kitchen prepares the food, the sommelier fetches wine and prepares the alcoholic beverages where applicable, and the waiter readies the service cart and prepares nonalcoholic drinks. The process then waits until all of the items required for this order are ready, after which the waiter delivers the order to the guest’s room. Following delivery, it is decided whether to bill immediately or defer: if billed now, the waiter debits the guest’s account and the process ends; if billing is deferred, billing is postponed until a later opportunity and then the waiter debits the guest’s account, after which the process ends.

1.text: The guest’s part begins when they place a call to room service and then their involvement ends; this call is received by the room‑service manager, who records the order and thereby starts the hotel’s workflow. From there, the manager launches three work streams at once: one sends the order ticket to the kitchen so the kitchen can prepare the food; a second assigns the order to a waiter, who readies the cart and prepares nonalcoholic drinks; and a third evaluates whether the order includes alcoholic beverages. If it does, the manager passes the beverage part to the sommelier, who prepares the alcoholic drinks; if it does not, the process explicitly confirms that no alcoholic beverages are included. Once food preparation, the waiter’s cart and nonalcoholic drinks, and either the alcoholic beverages or the confirmation of none are all complete, the waiter delivers the order to the guest’s room. After delivery, it is decided whether the waiter must handle another order first; if so, that is handled before proceeding, otherwise the process moves on directly to debiting the guest’s account, after which the hotel’s workflow ends.

2.text: The process begins when the guest initiates contact by calling room service, and this call is communicated to the room‑service manager, who begins their process by taking down the order. The manager then submits an order ticket to the kitchen and determines whether alcoholic beverages are requested. If alcoholic beverages are requested, the manager gives the order to the sommelier, after which two things happen: the sommelier prepares the alcoholic beverages, and the manager assigns the order to a waiter. If no alcoholic beverages are requested, the manager records that no alcoholic beverages are required and then assigns the order to a waiter while also marking the beverage branch as complete. The outcome of the beverage branch (either prepared alcoholic beverages or no‑alcohol confirmation) is then brought together with the other preparations. Once the waiter has been assigned, the waiter initiates parallel preparations: the kitchen prepares the food while the waiter readies the cart and prepares any nonalcoholic drinks. When the food is ready, the waiter’s preparations are complete, and the beverage branch has completed, all three converge and the waiter delivers the order to the guest’s room. After delivery, it is decided whether to bill immediately; if billing proceeds now, the guest’s account is debited at once, whereas if billing is deferred, billing is postponed and then the guest’s account is debited, after which the process ends.

The kitchen then prepares the food and waits at the point where all items must be ready. The waiter begins preparations by working on two activities in parallel—readying the cart and preparing nonalcoholic drinks—and once both are finished, this stream also reaches the all‑items‑ready point. If alcoholic beverages are needed, a beverage order is placed and the sommelier fetches wine and prepares the alcoholic beverages before joining at the all‑items‑ready point; if they are not needed, this path proceeds directly there. When all active paths have arrived, the waiter delivers the order to the guest room and then the guest’s account is debited, after which the hotel process ends.

0.text: Within MSPN, the process begins and immediately proceeds to send a dismissal to MSPO; once sent, that branch concludes. At MSPO, the process starts with receiving this dismissal and conducting a review. Based on the dismissal decision, MSPO either rejects the dismissal of MSPN and then finishes, or confirms the dismissal of MSPN and then finishes. The communication between the participants is a single transmission from MSPN’s sending of the dismissal to MSPO’s review, which initiates MSPO’s handling of the case.

1.text: In the MSPN lane, the process begins and proceeds with Send dismissal to MSPO; once sent, that branch concludes. In the MSPO lane, a separate start leads to Receive dismissal from MSPN, which corresponds to the dismissal sent by MSPN; after receipt, MSPO continues with Review dismissal. Based on the outcome of this review, a decision is taken: if the dismissal is not accepted, MSPO performs Reject dismissal of MSPN and then reaches the rejected end; if the dismissal is accepted, MSPO performs Confirm dismissal of MSPN and then reaches the confirmed end. The communication between the participants is captured by the dismissal sent from MSPN’s Send dismissal to MSPO to MSPO’s Receive dismissal from MSPN.

2.text: At MSPN, the process begins and proceeds immediately to send the dismissal to MSPO, after which the MSPN workflow ends. In parallel, at MSPO the process begins and the dismissal is received from MSPN. MSPO then reviews the dismissal and decides whether to reject or confirm it. If it is rejected, the rejection is carried out and the MSPO workflow ends on the rejection path. If it is confirmed, the confirmation is carried out and the MSPO workflow ends on the confirmation path. The only communication between the parties is the dismissal sent by MSPN to MSPO, which is received before MSPO performs the review and decision.

3.text: In the MSPN pool, the process starts and immediately proceeds to Send dismissal to MSPO; once this is done, that process ends. In parallel, the MSPO pool has its own start and moves to Review dismissal. After the review, a decision is made: if the outcome is to Reject dismissal, the flow continues to Reject dismissal and then ends; if the outcome is to Confirm dismissal, the flow continues to Confirm dismissal and then ends. The communication between the two pools occurs when Send dismissal to MSPO delivers the dismissal to Review dismissal.

4.text: At MSPN, the process begins and immediately proceeds with MSPN sending the dismissal to MSPO, after which MSPN’s part concludes. At MSPO, a separate process begins and, upon receiving the dismissal from MSPN, MSPO reviews the dismissal and then makes a decision. If the outcome is to reject, MSPO rejects the dismissal and ends; if the outcome is to confirm, MSPO confirms the dismissal and ends. The communication between the two parties occurs when MSPN sends the dismissal to MSPO, which is received and reviewed by MSPO.

5.text: In the MSPN participant, the process begins and proceeds to send the dismissal to MSPO; once sent, MSPN’s part concludes. The communication delivers the dismissal to MSPO, where, after its own start, the dismissal is reviewed. Based on the dismissal decision, the flow continues either by rejecting the dismissal or by confirming it. In both cases, once the respective action is completed, the MSPO process ends.

6.text: In the MSPN process, the work begins with the start and proceeds to Send dismissal; once this is completed, a message containing the dismissal is sent to the MSPO process, after which the MSPN process ends. In the MSPO process, work starts separately and moves to Review dismissal, where the received dismissal from MSPN is examined. A decision is then taken (Dismissal decision): if the outcome is to reject, the path continues with Reject dismissal and then concludes; if the outcome is to confirm, it proceeds with Confirm dismissal and then likewise concludes.

7.text: In the MSPN pool, the process starts and proceeds to Send dismissal to MSPO, after which it ends. This action communicates the dismissal to the MSPO pool. In the MSPO pool, the process starts and continues with Review dismissal, which considers the dismissal received from MSPN. Based on the dismissal decision, the flow either goes to Reject dismissal and then finishes at end (rejected), or it goes to Confirm dismissal and then finishes at end (confirmed).

8.text: The process involves two parties. On the MSPN side, it begins when MSPN sends the dismissal to MSPO; once this is sent, MSPN’s part of the process is complete. The communication delivers the dismissal to MSPO, where MSPO reviews the dismissal. Based on this review, MSPO makes a decision: either reject the dismissal of MSPN or confirm the dismissal of MSPN. In the rejection path, MSPO records the rejection and finishes. In the confirmation path, MSPO records the confirmation and finishes. Each of the two outcomes leads to the completion of MSPO’s process.

9.text: In the MSPN participant, the process starts and immediately proceeds to send a dismissal to MSPO; once this has been sent, MSPN’s process ends. In parallel, the MSPO participant has its own start, after which it receives the dismissal sent by MSPN via a communication from MSPN’s sending step to MSPO’s receiving step. MSPO then reviews the dismissal and makes a decision to either reject or confirm it. If rejected, MSPO performs the rejection of the MSPN dismissal and concludes with the rejected end. If confirmed, MSPO performs the confirmation of the MSPN dismissal and concludes with the confirmed end.

0.text: The process starts when the Secretariat receives a paper or faxed invoice in the central inbox, performs a short visual inspection, and forwards the invoice to the accounting employee. The accounting employee identifies the supplier, creates the invoice record in ACME Financial Accounting, checks the invoice items, and notes the relevant cost centers and managers on the docket, then sends an invoice copy and the docket to the first cost center manager. The cost center manager reviews the invoice copy for accuracy; if the items are accurate, the manager marks AP on the docket. If not, the manager rejects AP with a note and explanation on the docket, after which the invoice copy is sent back to accounting. When a manager has marked AP, it is checked whether all positions are AP: if not, the copy is forwarded to the next cost center manager and the review repeats; if all positions are AP, the invoice copy is sent back to accounting. Accounting receives the returned invoice copy from internal mail and checks whether all items are AP. If some items are not AP, accounting clarifies inconsistencies with the vendor by requesting clarification (communication sent to the vendor, who provides clarification back), receives the vendor’s clarification, consults cost center managers by phone or email if necessary, and then checks whether the issues are resolved; if not resolved, clarification with the vendor is repeated, and if resolved, the invoice copy is resent to the cost center managers so that they can review it again as before. If all items are AP when received in accounting, the invoice copy is forwarded to the Commercial Manager, who performs a commercial audit. If a complaint arises during this audit, the Commercial Manager resolves the complaint with the supplier by communicating the complaint to the vendor and receiving the vendor’s response, after which the commercial audit is performed again; if no complaint arises, the Commercial Manager issues approval for payment. It is then checked whether the amount exceeds EUR 20: if it does, the Board conducts a review and approval before the signed documents are received in the signature file; if it does not, the signed documents are received directly. Accounting then issues the payment instructions and closes the invoice instance in ACME Financial Accounting, which completes the process.

0.text: The process begins in the Functional Department when the head detects personnel requirements and reports the vacancy to the Personnel Department. In parallel, the HR process starts when the HR representative receives that vacancy report. HR then decides whether there are any questions before drafting the job description: if questions arise, HR requests clarifications, which prompts the Functional Department to receive the clarification request and provide the needed clarifications; HR receives those clarifications and reassesses whether more questions remain, repeating this exchange as necessary until HR proceeds without further questions. HR then drafts the job description and sends it to the Functional Department for review. The Functional Department receives the job description for review, conducts the review, and decides whether corrections are required: if corrections are needed, it requests corrections from HR; HR receives the correction request, applies the requested changes to the job description, and sends the revised version back for another review, repeating this cycle until the Functional Department approves the job description. Once the job description is approved, the Functional Department communicates the approval to HR and its part of the process concludes. Upon receiving the approval, HR advertises the position and completes its process.

1.text: In the Functional Department, the process begins when the Head detects personnel requirements and reports the vacancy to the Personnel Department, sending the vacancy report to the HR Representative. In the Personnel Department, the process starts upon receiving this report; a decision is made whether clarifications are needed. If clarifications are needed, the HR Representative requests them from the Head, who provides the clarifications; these are then received by HR, after which HR drafts the job description. If no clarifications are needed, HR proceeds directly to drafting. Once drafted, HR sends the job description to the Head for review. Back in the Functional Department, after having reported the vacancy, the Head reviews the job description upon receipt and decides whether to approve it. If not approved, the Head requests corrections and communicates this request to HR; HR revises the job description and sends it again for review, repeating this cycle until the Head approves. When the Head approves, the Functional Department process ends and the approval is communicated to HR, upon which HR advertises the job and completes its process.

2.text: The process begins in the Functional Department, where the Head of Department reports the vacancy to the Personnel Department. The HR colleague receives the vacancy report and determines whether clarifications are needed; if so, HR requests clarifications from the Head of Department, who provides the clarifications and sends them back to HR, after which HR prepares the job description. If no clarifications are needed, HR proceeds directly to prepare the job description. Once prepared, HR sends the job description to the Head of Department, who reviews it and decides whether corrections are needed. If corrections are required, the Head of Department requests them from HR, who revises the job description, updates the prepared document, and sends it back for review; this cycle of review, correction request, revision, and re-preparation may repeat until no more corrections are needed. When the Head of Department concludes that no corrections are necessary, they approve the job description and notify HR to advertise the position, after which the process ends.

3.text: The process begins with the Head of the Functional Department detecting personnel requirements and reporting the vacancy to the Personnel Department. The Head reviews the job description and decides whether corrections are needed: if so, the Head requests corrections from HR, who revises the job description and sends the revised version back for another review, repeating this cycle until no further corrections are needed. Throughout, communications occur as follows: the vacancy report is sent from the Head to HR to enable preparation; any clarification request from HR is sent to the Head, whose response is then sent back to HR to support preparation; the prepared description is sent from HR to the Head for review; any correction request is sent from the Head to HR to trigger the revision; and each revised description is sent from HR back to the Head for review.

Communications between the two departments occur at key handoffs: the vacancy report from the department head to HR; any HR questions sent to the department head and the clarifications provided in return; the job description sent by HR for review to the department head; and, from the review, either a request for corrections or an approval sent back to HR.

0.text: The process starts in MPON, where MPON sends the dismissal to MPOO. This communication is passed to MPOO, which triggers MPOO to review the dismissal. After the review, a decision is taken on whether to oppose or confirm: if MPOO opposes the dismissal of MPON, that opposition is carried out and the process ends; alternatively, if MPOO confirms the dismissal of MPON, that confirmation is carried out and the process ends. A message is exchanged from MPON to MPOO when MPON sends the dismissal and MPOO receives it for review.

tasks.name: MPOO opposes the dismissal of MPON
MPOO confirms the dismissal of MPON

1.text: The process involves two participants. In MPON, it begins at its start, where MPON sends the dismissal to MPOO and then concludes. In MPOO, it begins separately at its start; MPOO receives the dismissal sent by MPON, then reviews the dismissal. Based on that review, a decision is made: either MPOO opposes the dismissal or confirms the dismissal. If MPOO opposes it, the process proceeds to the opposition activity and then ends. If MPOO confirms it, the process proceeds to the confirmation activity and then ends. The only communication between the participants is the dismissal sent from MPON’s sending activity to MPOO’s receiving activity.

2.text: The process has two collaborating parts. In MPON, it begins with the start and immediately proceeds to send the dismissal to MPOO; once sent, MPON’s part finishes. That communication triggers MPOO’s part: MPOO starts, receives the dismissal sent by MPON, and reviews it. Based on the review, MPOO either opposes the dismissal of MPON or confirms the dismissal of MPON. Regardless of which of these two outcomes is chosen, MPOO then reaches the end of its part. The only communication between the parties is the dismissal sent from MPON’s sending step to MPOO’s reviewing step.

3.text: The procedure unfolds in two participating groups. In MPON, it begins when MPON prepares and sends the dismissal to MPOO; once this transmission is completed, MPON’s part concludes. In MPOO, a case is opened to review the received dismissal. Upon receiving the communication from MPON, MPOO proceeds with the review and then makes a decision on the dismissal. If the decision is to oppose the dismissal of MPON, MPOO carries out the opposition and then brings the case to a close. If the decision is to confirm the dismissal of MPON, MPOO performs the confirmation and then likewise closes the case.

4.text: The collaboration begins separately in two participants. In MPON, the process starts and immediately proceeds to send the dismissal to MPOO; once this is sent, MPON’s part concludes. In MPOO, a separate start leads to reviewing the received dismissal. After the review, a decision is made to either oppose or confirm. If the choice is to oppose, the path continues with opposing the dismissal of MPON and then reaches its corresponding conclusion. If the choice is to confirm, the path continues with confirming the dismissal of MPON and then reaches its respective conclusion. The communication between the participants consists of MPON sending the dismissal to MPOO, which is then taken up for review in MPOO.

5.text: The process begins with sending the dismissal to MPOO. This communication delivers the case to MPOO, where the dismissal is reviewed. After the review, a decision is taken to either oppose or confirm the dismissal. If the choice is to oppose, the dismissal is opposed and the process finishes at the end labeled “end - opposition.” If the choice is to confirm, the dismissal is confirmed and the process finishes at the end labeled “end - confirmation.”

6.text: Within MPON, the process begins when MPON performs “Send dismissal to MPOO,” after which MPON’s part concludes. This communication delivers the dismissal to MPOO, where a separate process begins with “Review dismissal.” Following the review, a decision is taken at “Dismissal decision”: if the outcome is to oppose, MPOO proceeds with “Oppose dismissal of MPON” and then concludes; if the outcome is to confirm, MPOO proceeds with “Confirm dismissal of MPON” and then concludes.

7.text: The process involves two participants. In MPON, it begins with the start and immediately proceeds to send the dismissal to MPOO; once sent, MPON’s part concludes. That sending is communicated to MPOO, where a separate process starts, receives the dismissal, and then reviews it. After the review, MPOO decides whether to oppose or to confirm the dismissal. If MPOO opposes, it carries out the opposition and then finishes. If MPOO confirms, it performs the confirmation and then finishes.

8.text: In the MPON stream, the work begins and immediately proceeds to sending the dismissal to MPOO; once it is sent, the MPON stream concludes. In parallel, the MPOO stream begins and, upon receiving the dismissal from MPON, conducts a review. Based on that review, a choice is made to either oppose or confirm the dismissal of MPON: if it is opposed, the action to oppose the dismissal of MPON is carried out and the MPOO stream ends; alternatively, if it is confirmed, the action to confirm the dismissal of MPON is carried out and the MPOO stream ends. The communication between the two streams consists of MPON sending the dismissal to MPOO for that review.

9.text: The process begins in MPON, where MPON sends the dismissal to MPOO. Upon receipt, MPOO reviews the dismissal. Based on the outcome of the decision on dismissal, MPOO either opposes the dismissal or confirms the dismissal; in both cases the process then concludes. The communication from MPON to MPOO is explicitly represented by sending the dismissal from the sending step in MPON to the reviewing step in MPOO.

0.text: The process begins when an expense report is received. Immediately after that, three tracks start in parallel. In the main track, it is checked whether the employee already has an account; if not, a new account is created before proceeding, otherwise it continues directly. The report is then reviewed for automatic approval. After this review, if the amount is less than $200, reimbursement is executed via direct deposit and this track ends. If the amount is $200 or more, the report is sent for supervisor approval; if the supervisor approves, reimbursement is executed via direct deposit and this track ends, while if the supervisor does not approve, a rejection email is sent and this track ends. In the second parallel track, after 7 days elapse, an “approval in-progress” email is sent and that track concludes. In the third parallel track, after 30 days elapse, a cancellation email is sent and that track concludes.

1.text: The process begins when an expense report is received. Immediately, two time-based tracks are scheduled: one to trigger after seven days and another after thirty days. In the main track, it is first checked whether the employee already has an account; if not, a new account is created before proceeding. The report is then reviewed for automatic approval. If the amount is under $200, the reimbursement is issued via direct deposit and the process concludes. If the amount is $200 or more, the report goes to the supervisor for a decision. If the supervisor rejects it, a rejection email is sent and the process concludes; if approved, the reimbursement is issued via direct deposit and the process concludes. Independently of these outcomes, after seven days from the start an “approval in progress” email is sent and that timed track ends, and after thirty days from the start a cancellation email is sent and that timed track ends.

2.text: The process starts and immediately proceeds along three concurrent paths. In the main path, the expense report is received and the employee’s account is verified; if the account already exists the case moves directly to a review for automatic approval, otherwise an employee account is created first and then the case is reviewed for automatic approval. Based on that review, either the reimbursement is executed via direct deposit, or the case is routed to a supervisor for review and approval. After the supervisor’s decision, an approval leads to reimbursement via direct deposit, while a rejection triggers a rejection email; either outcome completes the process normally. In parallel, a second path waits 7 days and then sends an approval‑in‑progress email, after which that notification path ends without influencing the main outcome. Also in parallel, a third path waits 30 days; if that delay elapses, a cancellation email is sent and the entire process is brought to an immediate end, terminating any other ongoing work.

After the review, if the amount is less than $200, the process reimburses to direct deposit and ends; if the amount is $200 or more, it goes to supervisor approval. Following that approval, if the supervisor approves, the process reimburses to direct deposit and ends; if the supervisor rejects, a rejection email is sent to the employee and the process ends. Independently of that, when 7 days have elapsed, an approval‑in‑progress email (7 days) is sent and that path ends, and when 30 days have elapsed, a cancellation email (30 days) is sent and that path ends.

Otherwise, when the completion notice arrives earlier, the parallel track ends and the main process concludes.

In parallel, after 7 days have elapsed, an “approval-in-progress” email is sent and that notification branch finishes. After 30 days have elapsed, a cancellation email is sent and the process is canceled. Any ending caused by reimbursement completion, rejection, or cancellation terminates the overall process and stops any other running branches.

0.text: The process begins for the customer when they bring the defective computer to the CRS. This handover is communicated to the CRS, where their process starts with checking the defect, then calculating the repair cost and handing it out to the customer. The cost information is sent to the customer, who then decides whether the costs are acceptable. If the customer does not accept, they take the computer home unrepaired and their part ends as unrepaired; if they accept, they conclude their part with the accepted decision and communicate this decision back to the CRS. The CRS records the customer’s decision and, if the decision is a rejection, ends their part on rejection. If the decision is an acceptance, the CRS proceeds by choosing a repair activity: either checking and repairing the hardware or checking and configuring the software. After that, they test the system’s functionality. If an error is detected during testing, they return to choosing a repair activity and continue iterating between repair and testing as needed; if no error is found, the CRS finishes with the repair completed.

tasks.name: Calculate and hand out repair cost

1.text: The process begins when the customer brings the defective computer to the service center. The case is then handed over to the service staff, who check the defect and subsequently provide the customer with a repair cost calculation. Based on this, the customer decides whether the costs are acceptable. If the customer declines, the customer takes the computer home unrepaired and the process ends. If the customer agrees, the service staff proceed with repair activities, choosing between checking and repairing the hardware or checking and configuring the software, in any order and selecting one at a time. After each chosen activity is completed, the system’s functionality is tested. If the test reveals an error, the process returns to selecting the next repair activity (again choosing between hardware or software) and repeats the cycle of performing the selected work and testing. This loop continues until no error is detected in the test, after which the process concludes. Throughout, the handover from the customer to the service staff occurs when the computer is brought in, and the cost calculation is handed from the service staff to the customer before the customer’s decision.

tasks.name: CRS hands out repair cost calculation

2.text: The process begins when the customer brings the defective computer to the service center. The customer’s handover triggers the service representative to check the defect, informed by the customer’s submission. The representative then provides a repair cost calculation to the customer, communicating the estimate to them. The customer reviews the calculation and decides whether the costs are acceptable. If the costs are not acceptable, the customer takes the computer home unrepaired and the process ends. If the costs are acceptable, the service center proceeds by selecting the next repair activity: either checking and repairing the hardware or checking and configuring the software. After the selected activity is completed, the work converges and the system’s functionality is tested. If an error is detected during testing, another repair activity is selected (again choosing between hardware repair and software configuration) and the cycle of repair followed by testing repeats until no error is detected. Once testing reveals no error, the process ends.

3.text: The process begins on the customer side when the customer brings the defective computer. After this, the customer receives a repair cost calculation and then decides whether the costs are acceptable. If the costs are not acceptable, the customer takes the computer home unrepaired and the customer process ends as unrepaired; if the costs are acceptable, the customer process ends as accepted. In parallel, the service provider starts when the defective computer is handed in: they check the defect and calculate the repair cost, then provide the calculation to the customer and wait to receive the customer’s decision. If the decision indicates not to proceed, the service provider process ends immediately. If the customer decides to proceed, the service provider selects the next repair activity, choosing either to check and repair the hardware or to check and configure the software. Whichever is chosen, the work continues with testing the system’s functionality. If the test reveals an error, the service provider returns to selecting the next repair activity and continues iterating through repair and test until no error is detected; once the test passes without errors, the service provider process ends. The interactions between the two parties are as follows: when the customer brings in the computer, the service provider is informed to begin diagnosing and costing; once the service provider has prepared the calculation, it is sent to the customer so the customer can receive it; after the customer makes the decision on the costs, that decision is sent back to the service provider to either stop work or proceed with the repair.

Provide repair cost calculation to customer

4.text: The process starts when the customer brings the defective computer to the CRS. After receiving it, the CRS checks the defect and then provides a repair cost calculation, which is sent to the customer. The customer reviews this calculation and decides whether the costs are acceptable. If the costs are not acceptable, the customer takes the computer home unrepaired and the process ends there. If the costs are acceptable, the customer approves the repair and communicates this approval to the CRS, where the approval is received. The CRS then selects the repair activity to perform, either checking and repairing the hardware or checking and configuring the software. Whichever of these is performed, the work converges and the CRS tests the system functionality. If an error is detected during testing, the process returns to the point where the repair activity is selected and another appropriate repair activity is performed; this cycle can repeat until testing no longer detects any error. If no error is detected, the process ends with the repair finished.

5.text: In the Customer pool, the process starts when the customer brings the defective computer, which is handed over to CRS. In the CRS pool, their process starts with checking the defect and then calculating the repair cost; once calculated, CRS provides the repair cost to the customer. The customer receives the repair cost calculation, decides on the repair costs, and then follows one of two paths: if the costs are not acceptable, the customer takes the computer home unrepaired and the customer process ends; if the costs are acceptable, the customer communicates acceptance to CRS and then the customer process ends. Upon having provided the cost, CRS waits for the customer’s decision; once the acceptance is received, CRS selects the appropriate repair activity and either checks and repairs the hardware or checks and configures the software. After either activity, CRS tests the system’s functionality. If an error is detected during testing, CRS returns to select the repair activity and repeats the appropriate repair work and testing; if no error is detected, the CRS process ends.

6.text: The process begins when the customer brings the defective computer. The CRS examines the defect and then provides the repair cost calculation to the customer. Based on this, a decision is made about whether the costs are acceptable. If they are not acceptable, the customer takes the computer home unrepaired and the process ends in the unrepaired outcome. If the costs are acceptable, the CRS proceeds by selecting the next repair activity, choosing either to check and repair the hardware or to check and configure the software. After whichever activity is selected, the CRS tests the system’s functionality. If the test reveals an error, the process returns to selecting the next repair activity, allowing another pass through hardware or software work as needed. If no error is detected after the test, the process completes with the repair finished. 7.text: At the Customer side, the process begins when the customer brings the defective computer to CRS, then reviews the repair cost and decides whether the costs are acceptable. If the costs are acceptable, the customer confirms acceptance to CRS; otherwise, the customer takes the computer home unrepaired. In CRS, the process starts when the computer is handed over and CRS checks the defect and calculates the repair cost, then hands out the repair cost calculation and awaits the customer’s decision. Based on that decision, if the repair is accepted, CRS selects the repair activity and either checks and repairs the hardware or checks and configures the software; in both cases, the system functionality is then tested. If an error is detected during testing, CRS goes back to select the repair activity again; if no error is detected, CRS finishes the repair. 1.text: The process begins with the customer perceiving a service degradation and sending the problem parameters to Customer Service. In Customer Service, the problem parameters are received, a problem report is entered into system T, the report is compared to the SLA, countermeasures and priorities are determined, and the customer’s significance is determined for the electronic service. If the customer is premium, an extra problem‑fix process is triggered; otherwise, Customer Service decides whether the assessed significance changes priorities: if so, countermeasures are re‑prioritized; if not, they proceed directly. In either case, Customer Service creates a detailed problem report and sends it to Service Management. In Service Management, the detailed report is received and its analyzability is assessed: if it can be analyzed there, the problem is analyzed, a trouble report is created, and a status report is produced; if not, the detailed report is sent to Resource Provisioning. In Resource Provisioning, upon receipt of the detailed report, they check for possible problems: if none are found, a normal service execution notification is created; if problems are detected, the problem is analyzed and a trouble report is created; in both cases a status report is created and sent back to Service Management. Service Management then receives the status report (either from its own analysis or from Resource Provisioning), prepares a final status report, determines countermeasures based on that status, and selects one of three paths: (1) send actual service performance to Customer Service and finish with no problem outstanding; (2) undertake minor corrective actions, then create and send a problem resolution report to Customer Service and finish on the minor‑fix path; or (3) create a request for automatic resource restoration and send this request to Resource Provisioning, after which Service Management waits to receive a troubleshooting report from Resource Provisioning and, upon receipt, creates and sends a problem resolution report to Customer Service and then finishes after the restoration path. In parallel, Resource Provisioning also starts a waiting period for a restoration request (maximum two days); if a request arrives in time, they track all possible errors, undertake corrective actions, create a troubleshooting report, and send it to Service Management; if no request arrives within two days, this branch ends due to timeout. Back in Customer Service, upon receiving actual service performance from Service Management and, separately, upon receiving the problem resolution report from Service Management, they proceed in parallel: one branch creates a customer report (covering performance and resolution) and sends it to the customer, while the other reports any SLA violation to Billing & Collections; after both branches complete, Customer Service ends. In Billing & Collections, the SLA violation report from Customer Service is received, billing is adjusted, and that function ends. On the customer side, after having sent the initial problem parameters, the customer later receives the report from Customer Service and then finishes. Communications between participants occur as follows: the customer sends problem parameters to Customer Service; Customer Service sends the detailed problem report to Service Management; when Service Management defers analysis, it sends the detailed report to Resource Provisioning; Resource Provisioning sends its status report to Service Management; Service Management sends actual service performance and, if applicable, a problem resolution report to Customer Service; when restoration is requested, Service Management sends the restoration request to Resource Provisioning, and Resource Provisioning later sends the troubleshooting report back to Service Management; Customer Service reports any SLA violation to Billing & Collections and sends the final customer report to the customer.

Based on this review, either the report proceeds to the treasurer for further checks, or it is returned to the employee to be edited. If it is returned, the employee edits the expense report and resubmits it for the supervisor to review again, repeating this cycle until the supervisor allows it to move forward. When the report reaches the treasurer, the receipts and matches are checked. From there, either the report is linked to the payment system for processing, or it is sent back to the employee for corrections. If corrections are requested by the treasurer, the report is returned to the employee, who makes the required edits and resubmits it to the supervisor for another review, after which it can reach the treasurer again. Once the treasurer allows processing, the report is linked to the payment system, the process waits for payment confirmation, and then the process ends.

6.text: The process begins when an employee purchases the required product or service and then submits an expense report with the listed items and receipts. Automated expense rules are applied to the submission before the supervisor reviews the expense report. At this point, a decision is made: if the supervisor does not approve, the employee edits the report based on the supervisor’s feedback and resubmits it for the supervisor to review again, repeating as needed. If the supervisor approves, the treasurer checks that the receipts match the listed items. Another decision follows: if the receipts are not all in order, the treasurer returns the report to the employee for corrections, after which the employee edits the report and it goes back to the supervisor’s review step. If everything is in order, the treasurer accepts the expenses for processing, the process links to the payment system, payment confirmation is awaited, and the process ends once confirmation is received.

9.text: The process begins when the employee makes the purchase of a product or service and then submits an expense report with receipts. The submission is sent to the supervisor for review, who examines the report and decides whether to reject or approve it. If rejected, feedback is sent back to the employee, who edits the expense report and resubmits it; the resubmission is sent again to the supervisor for another review and decision. If approved, the approval is sent to the treasurer, who checks the receipts against the report and determines whether the receipts are complete. 0.text: The process begins with the Customer transmitting switch-over data to Customer Service. Customer Service starts by receiving the customer data, entering it into the CRM, and comparing it against the internal database for completeness and plausibility; if errors are found, Customer Service corrects the data based on the error list and repeats the comparison until no errors remain. Customer Service then checks whether the customer already exists; if not, a new customer object is created, after which contract documents are prepared. Customer Service triggers an automated document check in the CIS; based on the returned result, if issues are detected, Customer Service analyzes and resolves the document generation issues, regenerates the documents, and triggers the check again, repeating until the check is positive. Once positive, Customer Service sends a confirmation document to the Customer and then requests supplier concurrence via the CIS. The CIS forwards the supplier concurrence request to the Grid Operator. The Grid Operator receives the request, checks for supplier concurrence, and, if there is a conflict, informs the suppliers, demands conflict resolution, and terminates the sales agreement with the Old Supplier before sending a response to Customer Service; if there is no conflict, the response to Customer Service is sent immediately. After responding, the Grid Operator transmits meter data to both Customer Service and the Old Supplier, computes the final billing, and sends it to the Old Supplier, then concludes its part. On receiving the grid response, Customer Service evaluates whether there are objections; if there are, the case is ended as blocked due to supplier concurrence. If there are no objections, Customer Service creates the CIS contract and waits for the Customer’s decision within seven days: if the Customer withdraws, Customer Service receives the withdrawal and ends the case accordingly; if instead the Customer sends a contract confirmation (optional), Customer Service receives the confirmation, then later receives the meter data from the Grid Operator, imports the meter data into the required systems, and concludes with the new customer won. In parallel on the Customer side, after sending the initial data the Customer receives the confirmation document and may either send a withdrawal within seven days or optionally send a contract confirmation to Customer Service; later, after the Old Supplier’s billing process concludes, the Customer receives the final bill and reviews the contract details. On the Old Supplier’s side, upon receiving the termination from the Grid Operator, the Old Supplier handles the termination, later receives the meter data and the final billing from the Grid Operator, sends the final bill to the Customer, and ends. Communications between parties occur as follows: the Customer’s initial data is sent to Customer Service; Customer Service triggers the CIS check and receives the result; Customer Service sends the confirmation document to the Customer; Customer Service requests supplier concurrence via the CIS, which forwards it to the Grid Operator; the Grid Operator sends its response to Customer Service, then sends meter data to both Customer Service and the Old Supplier, and later sends the final billing to the Old Supplier; the Grid Operator also sends the termination to the Old Supplier; the Old Supplier sends the final bill to the Customer; and the Customer may send either a withdrawal or a contract confirmation back to Customer Service.

2.text: The Customer begins by initiating a switch-over request and sending the required data to the New Supplier’s Customer Service. Customer Service receives the data, enters it into the CRM, and compares it for completeness and plausibility, correcting any errors until the data set is clean. If the person is not yet in the database, a new customer object is created; otherwise they proceed directly to preparing the contract documents. The documents are prepared and then automatically checked; if issues arise, they are analyzed, resolved, and the documents are regenerated until they pass the check. Customer Service then sends the confirmation document to the Customer, who receives it and reviews the contract to either withdraw or confirm, noting that confirmation can also occur automatically after seven days. In parallel, Customer Service sends a supplier concurrence request (via CIS) to the Grid Operator. The Grid Operator receives the supply request, checks supplier concurrence, and either responds directly when there is concurrence or, if there is none, informs the involved suppliers and demands conflict resolution, communicates with the Old Supplier and carries out the termination, and then sends a response comment back to Customer Service. Customer Service receives the Grid Operator’s response comment and, if objections are present, waits for further comments in a loop until no objections remain; once there are none, Customer Service creates the CIS contract. At the Customer’s decision point, if the Customer withdraws, they send a withdrawal notice to Customer Service, which is received and the Customer Service process ends. If the Customer confirms (or auto-accepts after seven days), they send the confirmation to Customer Service, which then receives power meter data from the Grid Operator and imports it, completing its process. Meanwhile, after communicating with the Old Supplier, the Grid Operator sends power meter data to both Customer Service and the Old Supplier and computes the final billing, sending final billing data to the Old Supplier before finishing its part. The Old Supplier, upon receiving the termination from the Grid Operator, then receives the meter data and the final billing data from the Grid Operator, creates the final bill, and sends it to the Customer. The Customer, in the confirmation path, finally receives the final bill, ending the Customer’s process; in the withdrawal path, the Customer’s process ends earlier after sending the withdrawal notice.

If issues are found, Customer Service corrects the errors based on an error list and repeats the comparison until the data quality is acceptable. Once the data is clean, Customer Service checks whether the customer already exists; if not, a new customer object is created, after which contract documents for the supplier switch are prepared and automatically checked in the CIS. If document generation causes issues, Customer Service analyzes and resolves them and regenerates the documents, then repeats the automated check until the documents are fine. Customer Service then sends a confirmation document to the Customer, who receives it and reviews the contract details before deciding whether to confirm or withdraw. Meanwhile, Customer Service sends a request to the Grid Operator to check for supplier concurrence. The Grid Operator receives this request, checks for objections, and if any are raised, informs the involved suppliers and demands conflict resolution before proceeding; in any case, the Grid Operator sends a response indicating no objections back to Customer Service, who waits for and receives this response and then creates the CIS contract. Customer Service then waits for the Customer’s decision within seven days: if the Customer confirms, they notify Customer Service, who receives the confirmation; if the Customer withdraws, they notify Customer Service, who receives the withdrawal and ends the process on their side with the withdrawal outcome; if no decision arrives within seven days, the process continues automatically as if accepted. For the accepted path (confirmation or auto-accept), Customer Service waits to receive meter data, then imports the meter data into the required systems and ends their part of the process. In parallel after sending the no-objection response, the Grid Operator sends a termination instruction to the Old Supplier, waits until the switch date (no more than ten days after start), then sends meter data to both Customer Service and the Old Supplier, and computes and sends the final billing to the Old Supplier before ending. The Old Supplier receives the termination instruction, then receives the meter data, then the final billing from the Grid Operator, and subsequently creates and sends the final billing to the Customer. On the Customer side, after either confirming or withdrawing, they eventually receive the final billing from the Old Supplier and their process ends.

4.text: The process begins when the customer initiates a switch-over request, transmits their data to Customer Service, then later receives the confirmation document, checks the contract details, and decides either to withdraw or to confirm (if no action is taken within seven days, confirmation is assumed); if they withdraw, the process ends for the customer, otherwise they will eventually receive their final billing and then finish. On the Customer Service side, upon start, the data is received, entered into the CRM, and compared with the internal customer database; if errors are found, an error list is used to correct them and the comparison is repeated until no errors remain. If the customer is not found, a new customer object is created; otherwise the flow continues directly to preparing the contract documents. The documents are then checked automatically; if generation issues occur, they are analyzed and resolved and the documents are regenerated, after which the automatic check repeats until the documents are OK. Once ready, the confirmation document is sent to the customer, and a request is sent to the grid operator. Customer Service then receives the operator’s response and determines whether there are objections: if objections exist, the case is put into wait/resolve handling until an updated response comment arrives; otherwise a CIS contract is created and the received meter data is imported into the required systems, after which Customer Service completes. The grid operator starts by receiving the supply permission request, checks for supplier concurrence, and sends a response comment back to Customer Service. If there is supplier concurrence, the operator informs the suppliers and demands resolution, and then finishes; if there is no concurrence, the operator proceeds to terminate the agreement with the old supplier, transmits the consumption report (meter data) both to Customer Service for import and to the old supplier, then computes and sends the final billing to the old supplier before finishing. The old supplier starts by receiving the concurrence notification from the grid operator, then receives the termination notice, the meter data, and the final billing from the grid operator, after which the old supplier creates and sends the final billing to the customer. The inter-organizational exchanges that occur are: the customer’s data is sent to Customer Service; Customer Service sends the confirmation document to the customer; Customer Service sends the supply request to the grid operator and later receives response comments from the operator; if concurrence exists, the grid operator informs suppliers and Customer Service handles the concurrence; if not, the grid operator sends a termination to the old supplier, sends the meter data both to Customer Service and the old supplier, and sends the final billing to the old supplier; finally, the old supplier sends the customer’s final billing, which the customer receives before ending.

If the documents fail the check, the issues are analyzed, the documents are regenerated, and the automated check is repeated until the documents are fine. If the customer withdraws, the customer communicates the withdrawal to Customer Service, which processes the withdrawal and finishes. Once the data is clean, Customer Service checks whether the customer already exists and, if not, creates a new customer object before preparing the contract documents and sending them to the CIS for an automated check. The CIS performs the automated check and returns the result to Customer Service; if the result is negative, Customer Service analyzes and resolves the causes of the failed generation, regenerates the contract documents, and resubmits them to the CIS until a successful result is achieved. When the check is successful, Customer Service sends the confirmation document to the Customer and the CIS sends a supplier request to the Grid Operator. The Customer receives the confirmation document, reviews the contract details, and then either sends a contract confirmation to Customer Service or sends a withdrawal; in parallel, Customer Service receives a response comment from the Grid Operator. If there are no objections from the Grid Operator, Customer Service creates the CIS contract and then waits for the seven-day withdrawal period to elapse; based on the Customer’s decision, if a withdrawal is received the Customer Service process ends, but if a confirmation is received or the waiting period expires without withdrawal, Customer Service proceeds to receive power meter data from the Grid Operator and imports it, then ends. After receiving the supplier request from the CIS, the Grid Operator checks supplier concurrence: it either sends a response comment back to Customer Service (reflecting objections) or, if proceeding, informs the suppliers and demands conflict resolution, communicates with the Old Supplier to terminate the sales agreement, then sends power meter data both to Customer Service and to the Old Supplier, computes the final billing, and sends it to the Old Supplier before ending its part. Triggered by the Grid Operator’s communications, the Old Supplier receives the termination instruction, receives the meter data and the final billing from the Grid Operator, then creates and sends the final billing to the Customer and ends. In a separate path, the Customer’s interaction concludes either after sending the confirmation or the withdrawal, and later the Customer receives the final billing from the Old Supplier and finishes.

9.text: The process begins with the customer submitting a switch-over request with the necessary data and then, once later contacted, reviewing the contract details to either withdraw from the contract or confirm it; if the customer withdraws, their part ends immediately, whereas if they confirm, they will eventually receive the final bill and then finish. The initial request data is sent to the new supplier’s customer service, which receives the customer data, enters it into the CRM, and compares it with the internal database for completeness and plausibility; if errors are found, they are corrected based on the error list and the comparison is repeated until no errors remain. At that point, if the customer is not already in the database, a new customer object is created before preparing the contract documents; otherwise, the preparation proceeds directly. The prepared documents undergo an automated check; if issues are detected, the team analyzes and resolves the document generation problems and regenerates the documents, after which the automated check is repeated until the documents are acceptable. Customer service then sends the confirmation document to the customer for review and, in parallel with the customer’s review, sends an eligibility request to the grid operator and awaits the response. The grid operator, upon receiving the eligibility request, checks for supplier concurrence or objections; if objections arise, it informs the involved suppliers and demands conflict resolution, then communicates with the old supplier to terminate the agreement before sending a response back to customer service; if there are no objections, it sends the response directly to customer service. After replying, the grid operator transmits meter data both to customer service and to the old supplier, computes the final billing, and sends the final billing to the old supplier before ending its part. The old supplier, after receiving the termination notice from the grid operator, processes the termination of the sales agreement, receives the meter data and then the final billing from the grid operator, and sends the final bill to the customer, after which it ends its part. Back at customer service, upon receiving the grid operator’s response, if there are objections the process ends at this stage; if there are no objections, a CIS contract is created, the customer is notified to review the contract, and the customer’s decision is received: if a withdrawal is recorded, customer service ends; if the customer accepts immediately, customer service proceeds to import meter data to the required systems; alternatively, if no immediate reply is given, customer service waits seven days and then accepts the contract and imports the meter data. Throughout, the confirmation document is sent from customer service to the customer for review, the customer’s withdrawal or confirmation is sent back to customer service, the eligibility request flows from customer service to the grid operator and the corresponding response returns, the grid operator sends meter data to both customer service and the old supplier, and the old supplier forwards the customer’s final bill to the customer, who receives it and concludes.

This communication triggers the supplier’s process with the order being received, after which the supplier processes the order and then sends an invoice to Assembler AG. Upon receiving the invoice, Assembler AG concludes its work. In parallel, once the supplier has dispatched the invoice, the supplier’s process also reaches its end.
